title: Trump pardons Jesse R. Benton
description_medium: On December 23, 2020, Donald Trump pardoned Jesse Benton, a senior operative in Ron Paul’s 2012 presidential campaign. Benton had been convicted in Iowa of conspiring to conceal payments made to secure state senator Kent Sorenson’s endorsement. The White House said he and co-defendant John Tate each received two years’ probation, including six months of home confinement.
description_long:
Jesse Benton’s pardon addressed his role in a campaign-finance scheme surrounding Ron Paul’s 2012 presidential bid. Federal prosecutors said Benton and fellow campaign official John Tate concealed more than $70,000 paid to Iowa state senator Kent Sorenson after Sorenson switched his endorsement to Paul. The payments were routed through companies and falsely reported as audiovisual expenses; a jury convicted Benton of conspiracy, false records and reporting, and false statements to the Federal Election Commission.

Trump granted Benton a full pardon on December 23, 2020, alongside Tate. The White House statement emphasized their six-month home-confinement terms, two years’ probation, and support from Senator Rand Paul and former FEC chair Lee Goodman, who argued the reporting rule was unclear at the time. The pardon erased Benton’s federal conviction’s remaining legal consequences; the stated clemency rationale relied on that support and disagreement over the clarity of the campaign-finance rules.
source_access_notes: White House clemency statement read for pardon date, support and sentence; DOJ trial announcement read for the payment scheme and convictions; DOJ clemency table read for listed offenses and sentence.
rationale: The 2016 DOJ announcement explains the concealed Sorenson payments; the December 2020 White House statement supplies the pardon date, supporters, and sentence. The separate later Benton conviction is not part of this pardon.

title: Trump pardons Joseph Martin Stephens
description_medium: Trump granted Joseph Martin Stephens a full pardon on December 23, 2020. Stephens’s federal conviction followed his 2008 guilty plea to possessing a firearm as a felon; the underlying felony dated to a state case when he was 19. He served 18 months in prison and three years of supervised release. The White House said business associates supported clemency.
description_long:
Joseph Martin Stephens received a full presidential pardon on December 23, 2020. His federal case stemmed from a 2008 guilty plea to possessing a firearm as a felon, after a 1991 state felony conviction when he was 19. The White House statement said Stephens had turned down deferred adjudication in the state case, later accepted responsibility for possessing the firearm, and served 18 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release.

The administration described support from Stephens’s business associates but gave no further account of their reasons or of a specific public campaign for clemency. The pardon therefore came after he had completed the sentence listed in the statement and removed the continuing federal disabilities attached to the conviction. The Justice Department’s clemency list records the case and sentence, while the White House account adds the age and chronology behind the conviction. The May 2018 date carried in the inherited record does not match the official December 2020 clemency announcement.
source_access_notes: White House clemency statement read for grant date, underlying conviction, age and sentence; DOJ clemency table read for case listing and sentence.
rationale: The White House statement identifies a December 23, 2020 pardon and supplies the conviction history; the DOJ list corroborates the case and sentence. The supplied 2018 date appears unrelated to the clemency grant.

title: Trump pardons Aviem Sella
description_medium: On January 20, 2021, Trump fully pardoned Aviem Sella, a retired Israeli Air Force officer indicted in 1986 for espionage connected to Jonathan Pollard. Sella recruited Pollard, a U.S. Navy intelligence analyst who passed classified information to Israel, and fled the United States after Pollard’s arrest. Israel sought the pardon as a step toward closing a long-running dispute.
description_long:
Aviem Sella was a retired Israeli Air Force officer indicted in the United States in 1986 on three espionage counts connected to the Jonathan Pollard case. Sella recruited Pollard, a Navy intelligence analyst who sold classified U.S. information to Israel, and left the country after Pollard was arrested in 1985. Israel did not extradite Sella, and the case became a source of tension between Washington and Jerusalem.

Trump issued Sella a full pardon on January 20, 2021, his final day in office. The White House said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and diplomatic officials supported the request, and that Israel had issued an apology and sought clemency to close the chapter in bilateral relations. Pollard, who had served 30 years in prison and was released on parole in 2015, publicly welcomed the pardon. The DOJ clemency list’s inherited date of May 2018 is not the date of this grant.
source_access_notes: White House statement read for pardon date and stated Israeli request; AP report read for Sella’s role, Pollard’s case, and diplomatic context; DOJ list read for the clemency entry.
rationale: The White House and AP identify a January 20, 2021 pardon; AP supplies the indictment and Pollard chronology. The inherited May 2018 date is inconsistent with the actual grant.

title: Trump pardons Casey Urlacher while federal gambling case is pending
description_medium: Trump granted Casey Urlacher a full pardon on January 20, 2021, while federal charges were pending. Prosecutors had accused the Mettawa, Illinois, mayor and nine others of operating an illegal offshore sports-betting business. Urlacher, brother of former Chicago Bears linebacker Brian Urlacher, had pleaded not guilty; the pardon came before any trial verdict.
description_long:
Casey Urlacher, the unpaid mayor of Mettawa, Illinois, was among those charged in a federal investigation of an offshore sports-gambling operation. An indictment accused Urlacher and nine others of conspiring to run the operation; he pleaded not guilty. The allegations had not been resolved at trial when Trump granted him a full pardon on January 20, 2021, the president’s final day in office.

The White House statement described Urlacher’s local public service and said friends, family, and community members supported clemency. It did not explain how those supporters addressed the pending gambling allegations. Contemporary reporting identified Urlacher as the brother of former Chicago Bears linebacker Brian Urlacher, a detail that drew attention to the pardon. The clemency ended the federal prosecution against him without a jury verdict or sentence, a key distinction from pardons granted after conviction. The inherited May 2018 date predates the indictment and is not the pardon date.
source_access_notes: White House statement read for pardon date and administration’s stated support; CBS Chicago report read for pending charges, not-guilty plea, and family relationship; DOJ clemency table consulted for the recipient record.
rationale: CBS Chicago confirms the pending charges and not-guilty plea; the White House statement dates the full pardon to January 20, 2021. The case had no trial verdict when clemency was granted.

title: Trump pardons Robert Zangrillo in pending college-admissions case
description_medium: Trump pardoned Miami developer Robert Zangrillo on January 19, 2021, while his Varsity Blues case was awaiting trial. Prosecutors alleged he paid $250,000 through consultant Rick Singer and USC athletics administrator Donna Heinel to secure his daughter’s admission. Zangrillo pleaded not guilty and disputed that the payment was a bribe; no trial verdict preceded the pardon.
description_long:
Robert Zangrillo, a Miami real-estate developer, was charged in the Varsity Blues college-admissions investigation. Prosecutors alleged that he paid $50,000 to USC’s athletics department and $200,000 to consultant Rick Singer as part of a plan to secure his daughter’s admission through a purported rowing-recruit profile. Zangrillo pleaded not guilty, and his lawyers argued that the university donation was not a bribe. His case was awaiting trial when Trump granted him a full pardon on January 19, 2021.

The White House described Zangrillo as a philanthropist and said his daughter had not had others take standardized tests for her and was earning a 3.9 GPA at USC. The Los Angeles Times reported that USC said she was not then enrolled, and that a spokesperson for supporter Tom Barrack denied intervening in the pardon. Zangrillo was the only defendant in the college-admissions case to receive a pardon, according to the Times. The grant came before a verdict, so the prosecution’s allegations were not findings of guilt; the clemency statement did not provide a case-specific explanation for Trump’s decision.
source_access_notes: White House statement read for clemency grant and administration’s description; Los Angeles Times report read for prosecutors’ allegations, defense response, Barrack denial, and USC enrollment information; DOJ clemency table read for grant date.
rationale: The DOJ list dates the pardon to January 19, 2021; the Times details the pending case and reports both the White House claim about USC enrollment and the university’s contrary account. The allegations were unresolved at trial.
